subject: psychology
topicDisplay: Applied Psychology Options Child Criminal Environmental Sport And Exercise
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: According to learning theory, how is attachment explained through classical conditioning?
options: The infant imprints on the caregiver during a critical period
An internal working model forms a template for relationships
The caregiver (neutral stimulus) becomes associated with food (unconditioned stimulus) to produce pleasure
The infant is positively reinforced by the removal of discomfort
questions.explain: In classical conditioning the caregiver becomes a conditioned stimulus by being repeatedly paired with the pleasure of food.

questions.q: Bowlby's maternal deprivation theory linked offending to:
options: Early separation from the mother producing an affectionless psychopath
questions.explain: Bowlby's 44 thieves study linked early maternal deprivation to affectionless psychopathy and delinquency.

questions.q: An infant classified as 'insecure-avoidant' (Type A) in the Strange Situation typically shows:
options: Low anxiety, willing exploration and little reaction to the caregiver's departure or return
High stranger and separation anxiety and resistance at reunion
Moderate anxiety and easy comfort at reunion
questions.explain: Type A infants explore freely, show little separation distress and largely ignore the caregiver on reunion.

questions.q: According to differential association, a person becomes an offender when:
options: Pro-criminal attitudes learned outweigh anti-criminal attitudes
questions.explain: Sutherland argued offending results when the number of favourable definitions toward crime exceeds unfavourable ones.

questions.q: Bandura's social learning theory explains aggression as acquired through:
options: Observation, imitation and vicarious reinforcement of models
questions.explain: SLT holds that aggression is learned by observing models, with imitation more likely when the model is reinforced (vicarious reinforcement).

questions.q: The three stages of Novaco's anger management/stress inoculation are:
options: Cognitive preparation, skill acquisition, application practice
questions.explain: Stress inoculation training progresses through cognitive preparation, skill acquisition (e.g., relaxation), and application practice in role-play.

questions.q: Zeanah et al.'s Bucharest Early Intervention study found that institutionalised children most often showed which attachment type?
questions.explain: In the Bucharest study a high proportion of institutionalised children were classified as disorganised in attachment.

questions.q: What is meant by 'interactional synchrony'?
options: The infant showing distress on separation from the caregiver
The caregiver and infant taking turns to respond alternately
The caregiver and infant mirroring each other's actions and emotions in a coordinated, simultaneous way
The infant developing a routine of feeding times
questions.explain: Interactional synchrony is the simultaneous, coordinated mirroring of actions and emotions between caregiver and infant.

questions.q: Anger management programmes for offenders are based on which approach?
questions.explain: Anger management is a CBT-based programme (often using Novaco's stress inoculation: cognitive preparation, skill acquisition, application practice).

questions.q: The dispositional (importation) model of institutional aggression argues that violence in prisons is due to:
options: Characteristics inmates bring into the institution
questions.explain: The importation model says inmates import their own dispositions (e.g., values, history) that lead to aggression, contrasting with the situational deprivation model.

questions.q: In Eysenck's theory, criminal behaviour also reflects poor socialisation because high E and N scorers are:
options: Easier to condition into prosocial norms
More difficult to condition, so they fail to develop a strong conscience
questions.explain: Eysenck argued conscience is conditioned; people high in E and N condition poorly, so they less readily learn to avoid antisocial behaviour.

questions.q: What did Schaffer and Emerson find regarding the formation of multiple attachments?
options: By one year, most infants had formed multiple attachments
Multiple attachments formed before specific attachments
Infants never form attachments to more than one person
Multiple attachments only formed in institutionalised children
questions.explain: By around one year of age the majority of infants in the study had developed multiple attachments to several people.

questions.q: In Schaffer and Emerson's (1964) Glasgow study, at roughly what age did most infants form their first specific attachment?
questions.explain: Schaffer and Emerson found that specific attachments typically formed at around seven months, shown by separation and stranger anxiety.

questions.q: Berkowitz's reformulation of frustration-aggression added the idea that:
options: Frustration creates readiness, but cues (e.g. weapons) are needed to trigger aggression
Aggression is unrelated to the environment
questions.explain: Berkowitz argued frustration produces anger/readiness, and aggressive cues in the environment (the 'weapon effect') make aggression more likely.

questions.q: 'Minimalisation' as a cognitive distortion involves:
options: Downplaying the seriousness or consequences of an offence
questions.explain: Minimalisation reduces the offender's feelings of guilt by underplaying the harm caused (e.g., describing theft as 'borrowing').

questions.q: In Eysenck's theory of the criminal personality, the high-scoring offender is typically:
options: High in extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism
questions.explain: Eysenck proposed the criminal personality is high on extraversion, neuroticism and (later) psychoticism.

questions.q: A characteristic effect of institutionalisation reported in Romanian orphan studies is:
options: Reduced stranger anxiety in adulthood only
questions.explain: Disinhibited attachment, marked by indiscriminate affection towards strangers, was a common effect of institutional care.

questions.q: Bowlby's 'social releasers' are best described as:
options: Behaviours measured in the Strange Situation
Innate behaviours such as smiling and cooing that elicit caregiving
questions.explain: Social releasers are innate infant behaviours like smiling that trigger an adult caregiving response and promote attachment.

questions.q: What did Lorenz conclude about imprinting and timing?
options: Imprinting can occur at any point in life
Imprinting must occur within a critical period or it will not occur at all
Imprinting only occurs after the first month
questions.explain: Lorenz argued imprinting must take place within a fixed critical period, after which it would not happen.

questions.q: Behaviour modification in custody is based on:
options: Operant conditioning, using a token economy to reinforce desirable behaviour
questions.explain: Behaviour modification uses operant conditioning: tokens (secondary reinforcers) are given for target behaviours and exchanged for privileges.

questions.q: Van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg's (1988) meta-analysis of cultural variations found that:
options: Resistant attachment was most common everywhere
Secure attachment was the most common type across all cultures studied
Attachment types were identical in every culture
questions.explain: Across the 32 studies, secure attachment was the modal type in every culture, though insecure proportions varied.

questions.q: Bowlby's 'law of continuity' states that:
options: The more constant and predictable a child's care, the better the attachment quality
Attachment is continuous across all caregivers
questions.explain: The law of continuity states that consistent, predictable care leads to better-quality attachment.

questions.q: In van IJzendoorn's meta-analysis, where was insecure-resistant attachment notably higher and insecure-avoidant lower?
questions.explain: Collectivist samples such as Japan and Israel showed higher rates of resistant and lower rates of avoidant attachment.

questions.q: In Ainsworth's original sample, which attachment type was the most common?
questions.explain: Secure attachment (Type B) was the most common classification, found in around two-thirds of infants.

questions.q: Restorative justice programmes primarily aim to:
options: Repair harm by involving the victim and encouraging offender responsibility
Maximise the length of custodial sentences
questions.explain: Restorative justice focuses on healing for the victim and rehabilitation of the offender through accountability, often via supervised meetings.

questions.q: Which behaviours did the Strange Situation assess?
options: Proximity-seeking, exploration/secure-base, stranger anxiety, separation anxiety and reunion behaviour
questions.explain: Ainsworth recorded proximity-seeking, secure-base exploration, stranger anxiety, separation anxiety and reunion behaviour.

questions.q: In Kohlberg's moral reasoning, many offenders are found to reason at the:
questions.explain: Offenders often reason at the pre-conventional level, motivated by avoiding punishment and gaining reward rather than internalised morality.

questions.q: In Lorenz's ethological account, aggression is triggered by an innate releasing mechanism that produces a:
questions.explain: Lorenz argued a sign stimulus activates an innate releasing mechanism, producing a stereotyped, unchanging fixed action pattern.

questions.q: Bowlby's maternal deprivation hypothesis argues that prolonged separation in early life can lead to:
questions.explain: Bowlby linked maternal deprivation to affectionless psychopathy and low IQ, as suggested by his 44 thieves study.

questions.q: According to Schaffer and Emerson's stages of attachment, which stage comes immediately before specific attachment?
questions.explain: The order is asocial, indiscriminate, specific, then multiple attachments, so indiscriminate attachment precedes specific attachment.
